None had returned, however, since her son vanished at sea. The tide brought bottles, envelopes, whispered names, and old rumors. She wrote down their descriptions inside a worn leather notebook. The pages smelled faintly of salt, tobacco, and winter rain.

He could hear a spring surrendering before it suddenly fell. Patience, he often told customers, was time itself made visible. His young daughter, Mara, laughed at all such solemn definitions. She asked why damaged time could not simply be repaired. Tomas only smiled and carefully tightened another tiny brass screw. Mara grew restless whenever the little workshop became completely quiet. Outside, gulls quarreled above the brightening rooftops and crooked antennas.

She placed the small compass beside his largest wooden workbench. Tomas inspected it without asking why she had suddenly come. The needle spun lazily, as if uncertain about north tonight. He found a cracked glass and a weak magnetic core. It could be mended, he said, but never quite perfectly. The woman nodded slowly, as though expecting exactly that answer. Then she asked whether he remembered their old blue orchard.

He did remember, though memory had softened all its colors. As children, they planted apple trees behind their grandmother’s house. In spring, the branches filled with pale and impossible blossoms. They called the place blue because storms arrived before noon. Lightning illuminated the whole orchard in flashes of violet light. They raced between trees, counting thunderclaps and daring each other. That autumn, a terrible storm tore half the orchard away. She had been trapped beneath the collapsed stone boundary wall. Tomas had pulled her free and lost his blue coat. They had promised to return together after the first snow.

He repaired the compass because her visits revived old memories. She returned every autumn, always arriving near the closing time. They spoke of ordinary things: weather, rents, distant relatives, books. Yet beneath all those easy conversations, old questions waited patiently. Did she regret leaving? Did he ever resent staying there? Neither answered directly, and neither of them lied about it. Between them, silence slowly became another kind of old clock.

The woman opened the rusty door, and dust breathed outward. Inside, clusters of blue fruit glowed faintly on neglected branches. Tomas frowned, carefully examining roots curled around several dark stones. He took the fruit and turned it beneath the light. Its skin was cool, smooth, and seemed almost faintly luminous. When he cut it, the juice shone like captured evening.

The woman watched him with guarded, quietly searching brown eyes. “Do you remember this flavor?” she asked, offering him half. Tomas closed his eyes as buried memories suddenly broke open. They were children again, racing through wind, lightning, and thunder. He could feel rain soaking through his missing blue coat. She was laughing somewhere beyond the crumbling stone orchard wall. Tears ran down Tomas’s weathered face, though he denied them. Mara looked between them and understood less than she imagined.
